findings.title: Findings converge on how readers resolve an index's flagged state
findings.why_it_matters: The mechanism is how each surface works out an index's flagged state from two stores: the instance map entry and the new needs-restart record. As designed, every reader does that fold itself. That covers about ten event emit sites, `get_snapshot`, `build_manifest_info`, `overlay_runtime_state`, `_emit_stopped_events`, the `AppStatus` tally and `AppStatusSnapshot.running_count`. Precedence ("the record wins") is defined only for `build_manifest_info`. Finding 3 (events drop the flag at any site that forgets it), Finding 4 (each reader re-derives "flagged" and the counts disagree) and Finding 5 (what an event or a count says when a live replacement sits at a flagged index) are three local symptoms of that one choice, raised by both critics. Should the read side of the record be re-evaluated as a whole rather than patched per reader? That re-evaluation includes whether every surface needs the flag at all, and which disagreements are worth handling before #3110's gate removes the live-replacement case.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate how the needs-restart record is read before addressing Findings 3, 4 and 5 individually. Open questions: should one registry operation own an index's effective state for snapshots, counts and events? Does the bus payload (`AppStateChangePayload`) need the flag at all, or only the WS and REST surfaces? What does any surface say for a flagged index with a live replacement until #3110 lands? Which of these disagreements are worth handling for the interim, and which are a limitation to document?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate how the needs-restart record is read before addressing Findings 3, 4 and 5 individually.
findings.choice_reason: Resolver + WS-dispatcher stamp; interim state never ships (no release until milestone complete), so record wins with no special case

findings.title: Findings converge on where `shutdown_instance` decides to flag
findings.why_it_matters: The mechanism is the owner-side flag decision: `_stop_*_unlocked` unregisters the instance, then `shutdown_instance` decides to flag from whichever branch of its `try/except Exception` ran. Finding 6 (REST shows STOPPED during the stop because the entry is already gone), Finding 7 (a cancelled owner never reaches the write) and Finding 8 (the raised branch guesses "a bad report exists" from "an exception occurred") all come from the decision living in exception branches after an early unregister. Each proposes its own patch to that block: a provisional record, a cancellation branch, a three-way split. Should the decision point be re-evaluated rather than patched branch by branch? Two of the three are rare, so accepting them as limitations is a legitimate outcome of that re-evaluation.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the current decision point and address Findings 6, 7 and 8 individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the current decision point and address Findings 6, 7 and 8 individually.

findings.title: Flag delivery depends on every emit site passing it
findings.why_it_matters: The design threads `needs_restart` into events through a new `emit_app_state_change` parameter "the emit sites fill from `AppRegistry`". Several sites bypass that helper and build `HassetteAppStateEvent` directly. Examples are `stop_one`'s STOPPING event, the NOT_STARTED events and the `from_instance_info` resyncs, plus `testing/_simulation.py`. The frontend replaces the whole store entry on each event. So any event for a flagged index that omits the object makes the badge vanish while REST still says flagged, and the design itself notes that "a field missed at any hop is silently dropped". An optional parameter defaulting to `None` makes that omission silent. Separately, `needs_restart_count` on the app summary only refreshes on `apps_changed` or reconnect, so the app-level count lags the per-instance badge.
findings.recommended: A: `RuntimeQueryService.on_app_state_changed` stamps `needs_restart` (and the flagged-index status rule) from `AppRegistry` when it builds `AppStatusChangedData`. `AppStateChangePayload` does not gain the field, and `emit_app_state_change` gains no parameter.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The instance entry and the record are two stores each reader folds on its own
findings.why_it_matters: Per-index state now lives in `_instances[app_key][index]` and the new record. They are written at different times and cleared by different operations: `unregister_app`, `prune_stale_failed_indices` and `record_failure` touch only the entry. The design lists the readers in prose. Each will re-derive "flagged" independently, and the existing counts already disagree on what "running" means. `AppStatusSnapshot.running_count` is "no recorded error", so a live replacement over a flagged index counts as running there, but as not running in the manifest tally the design specifies. The design also doesn't say which error text a flagged row shows once its failure entry is discarded.
findings.recommended: A: Add one `AppRegistry` method that returns an index's effective `AppInstanceInfo` (entry folded with record, the record's `reason` as the error when the entry is gone). Route `get_snapshot`, `build_manifest_info`, `get_failed_instance_infos`, `_emit_stopped_events`, `needs_restart_count`, the `AppStatus` tally and `running_count` through it.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A live replacement at a flagged index before #3110: what does it show?
findings.why_it_matters: Until #3110's gate lands, `reload_instance` stops a flagged instance and creates a live replacement at the same index. The design has the record win in `build_manifest_info`: FAILED plus `needs_restart` overlay a replacement that is initialized and serving, and it counts as not running. Nothing defines what the replacement's own events say. If they carry RUNNING plus the flag, the frontend (which prefers the WS status) shows RUNNING with a badge while REST and the CLI show FAILED. The ERROR tells the user to restart hassette. The natural move is reload instead, which works and runs two copies of the app's work (the zombie and the replacement), with no way to clear the FAILED badge short of a restart. The record also keeps the old instance's name and class if config renamed it.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: REST and CLI show STOPPED while a stop's hook is still running
findings.why_it_matters: D4's deciding factor is "never show stopped while work may still run". `_stop_app_unlocked` and `_stop_instance_unlocked` call `registry.unregister_app` before `shutdown_instances`. For the whole stop, up to the ~25 s entry deadline (45 s total minus the 20 s foundation budget), the index has no entry, and `build_manifest_info` fills it with a synthetic STOPPED placeholder. So REST and the CLI report STOPPED while `on_shutdown` is hung. The WS shows STOPPING, but only until a refetch. The flag lands only after the outcome is known, so the design's invariant holds for settled states but not during the stop.
findings.recommended: A: Unregister after the stop settles. `_stop_app_unlocked`/`_stop_instance_unlocked` read the running instances, shut them down, then unregister (or `record_failure` replaces the entry when flagged), so readers see the instance's own STOPPING status throughout.
findings.chosen: A: Unregister after the stop settles.
findings.choice_reason: Verified safe first: single shielded shutdown attempt, tighten-only deadline; accept duplicate exit-time ERROR rather than dedupe

findings.title: A cancelled owner mid-teardown leaves no flag, no failure entry and no ERROR
findings.why_it_matters: `shutdown_instance` catches only `Exception`. A `CancelledError` delivered while it waits in `asyncio.wait([task], timeout)` escapes. `asyncio.wait` does not cancel the inner shutdown task, so the teardown keeps running, but the owner never reaches the flag write, `record_failure`, the walk-away (`_force_terminal`, `record_force_terminated`) or the ERROR. On the runtime stop path the instance is already unregistered (Finding 6). That leaves the silent state the Posture forbids.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a stop whose caller is cancelled mid-teardown leaves the instance unflagged and logs no ERROR.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a stop whose caller is cancelled mid-teardown leaves the instance unflagged and logs no ERROR.

findings.title: The raised-shutdown branch infers the flag from "an exception occurred"
findings.why_it_matters: The design says the `except Exception` branch "flags the instance", because the coordinator stored a `COORDINATOR_FAILED` report. That try wraps much more than the coordinator: `tighten_shutdown_deadline`, `create_lifecycle_task`, `walk_away_from_instance`, and the STOPPED emit after a clean stop. If the branch flags unconditionally, an exception after a clean STOPPED marks a safe instance sticky-FAILED for the life of the process. If it flags only when a stored report satisfies the predicate, a failure before the coordinator ran leaves no flag, even though nothing was torn down.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an exception in `shutdown_instance` outside the coordinator can flag a clean instance or leave an untorn-down one unflagged.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: Merge-on-reflag grows the record and mixes evidence from different instances
findings.why_it_matters: Re-flagging an index "keeps the first `flagged_at`, appends the new reason, and merges the pending task names". The record is keyed `(app_key, index)` and never cleared. Each reload of a hung app before #3110 appends another reason and more task names to a payload that goes out on every `/api/apps` response and WS event (D7), with no cap. The merged record also mixes two physical instances. The reason and tasks describe the latest one, while `flagged_at` dates the first, and the record can't say which tasks belong to which instance.
findings.recommended: A: Drop the merge rule. The first record at an index stands until restart, and a later flag at that index logs its own ERROR naming its tasks.
findings.chosen: A: Drop the merge rule.
findings.choice_reason: Re-flag only exists in the unreleased interim before #3110

findings.title: `clear_all`'s effect on the needs-restart record is unstated
findings.why_it_matters: The design says only a process restart clears the record, but `AppRegistry.clear_all()` is called from process exit (`shutdown_all`) and from the test harness reset (`testing/_reset.py`). If `clear_all` leaves the record, a harness that resets between tests carries one test's flags into the next, so users' own test suites see FAILED rows they didn't cause. Both critics ask for one sentence settling it.
findings.chosen: Add one bullet to the design's Assumed section stating clear_all() clears the needs-restart record.

findings.title: At process exit, a flagged instance's ERROR says "restart hassette"
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: operator watching logs on shutdown. `shutdown_all` stops every instance through `shutdown_instance`. Under the design, every instance whose report satisfies the predicate takes the FAILED/ERROR branch with "stopped but work is still running: <tasks>; restart hassette", telling the operator to restart a process that is already exiting. `shutdown_instance` has no explicit exit-path signal.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: at process exit, a flagged instance's ERROR still says to restart hassette.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: "Init failed or timed out" stands in for "`on_initialize` never completed"
findings.why_it_matters: The skip-hooks flag is set from which `except` clause ran, and two cases break that proxy. (1) The outer `fail_after` fires while the shielded init task keeps running; if the init completes before the shutdown's `_observe_active_initializer` cancels it, the app is fully initialized but its `on_shutdown` is skipped. (2) `_initialize_body` initializes children after the user hooks, so a `Bus`/`Scheduler` init failure comes after `on_initialize` succeeded. The Assumed bullet that a failed init leaves children `NOT_STARTED` does not hold there. In both cases, resources the user opened outside the task bucket stay open until restart. The prior-art brief's Pattern 1 notes that HA and OTP decide the skip from state ("setup completed"), not from a per-attempt flag.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an init that completes right after its timeout, or whose framework child fails after `on_initialize` succeeded, has its `on_shutdown` skipped, so resources it opened outside the task bucket stay open until restart.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: Pending tasks are never re-checked, so a finished straggler reads as leaked work
findings.why_it_matters: The record stores task names, but nothing watches them. A task that finishes a second after the report still leaves the instance sticky-FAILED, with an ERROR that says work is still running and no later line saying it stopped. An operator can't tell a leaked loop from a slow HTTP call that ended long ago. The critic asks only for a diagnostic: an INFO log, and optionally a `settled_at`, when the named tasks finish. Clearing the flag is not part of the ask.
findings.chosen: Side B: no observation (ledger 134 as ratified)

findings.title: The failed-init listener/job cleanup guarantee rests on code reading
findings.why_it_matters: D3's choice depends on never-initialized `Bus`/`Scheduler` children still removing the failed app's listeners and jobs in their `on_shutdown`. The Assumed section cites only code reading. A child shutdown that raises carries `CHILD_SHUTDOWN_FAILED` and flags, so that path holds. The residual risk is a removal callback that ran partially without raising, leaving a DB listener or job row that nothing flags and only a later reconcile retires.
findings.chosen: Side A: spell out the observable assertion

findings.title: Failed-init teardown breaks the `startup_timeout_seconds >= app_startup_timeout_seconds` budget
Redefining `is_restart_safe` makes raised-body and cleanup-failure teardowns re-initializable for framework services

note: post-revise pass; hash taken after fixes

findings.title: A raised or cancelled shutdown body (`SHUTDOWN_BODY_FAILED`) now reads restart-safe
findings.why_it_matters: When the shutdown body raises or is cancelled, the coordinator throws away whatever the body collected and replaces it with a bare `SHUTDOWN_BODY_FAILED` report (lifecycle.py:668-675). Any `pending_tasks` from the task-bucket stage are lost, and child shutdown may never have run. `SHUTDOWN_BODY_FAILED` is not in `WORK_MAY_RUN_CAUSES` (teardown.py:78-87), so the redefined `is_restart_safe` returns True. On main, any cause made a report unsafe (`return not self.causes`). The result: an instance whose teardown proved nothing shows STOPPED (or FAILED "timed out, nothing pending") with no flag, it can be reloaded, and `start()`/`initialize()` no longer raise `RestartRefusedError` over live tasks. That is the "stopped while work may run" state D4 rules out. The shipped docs also promise the opposite: operating/index.md:207 says an instance is flagged when "part of the teardown fails in a way that leaves no proof the work stopped". Ledger 134 D18 (design.md:647 of spec 134) did classify "raised or timed-out hooks, bodies and cleanups" as diagnostic, on the premise that the failed step "was cancelled and has ended". For a body, the coroutine has ended, but the stages it never reached haven't, and the report no longer records which tasks were pending. So the ratified premise does not hold for this one cause.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a shutdown body that raises or is cancelled reads restart-safe, and the docs bullet is reworded to say so.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation
findings.choice_reason: Leaning 'less is more'; asked what peers do — AppDaemon and Node-RED treat a raised teardown as stopped

findings.title: Stop/reload of any app with a flagged index always answers 500 ACTION_FAILED, even when the action succeeded
findings.why_it_matters: `_raise_if_target_failed` (routes/apps.py:301-325) reads `get_failed_instance_infos`, which now includes every flagged index until restart (app_registry.py:294-303). So:
findings.recommended: A: Exclude indices that were already flagged before the action from `_failed_target_instances`'s verdict, fix the `stop never matches` docstring, and add a route test for a whole-app stop with a flagged sibling and for a flagged-only stop.
findings.chosen: C: Leave as is and add these cases to #3110

findings.title: The PR needs a breaking-change marker for the removed config key and the redefined `is_restart_safe`
findings.why_it_matters: `failed_instance_cleanup_timeout_seconds` is now rejected at load, so a config that sets it fails to load. `TeardownReport.is_restart_safe`, a documented property (docs/pages/core-concepts/internals/lifecycle.md:112-124), changes meaning: reports with only a raised or timed-out hook or a failed cleanup now read True, and `_on_children_stopped` fires in those cases. CLAUDE.md requires `feat!:` with exactly one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer for a breaking change. No branch commit carries `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE` footer (`git log main..HEAD`), and the squash-merged PR title becomes the changelog line.
findings.chosen: Title the PR `feat!: ...`, and end the PR body with a single `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer that covers both the removed `failed_instance_cleanup_timeout_seconds` key and the new meaning of `is_restart_safe` ("no work may still be running").

findings.title: `AppSync` hook timeouts stay unflagged while the docs say a hook that ended has nothing left running
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: apps built on `AppSync` that wrap blocking libraries. Sync worker threads are out of the predicate's scope (ledger Summary; 134 D18), so the code gap itself is accepted. The docs, however, now overclaim:
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the needs-restart flag doesn't cover an `AppSync` hook's worker thread, and the docs don't say so.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: the needs-restart flag doesn't cover an `AppSync` hook's worker thread, and the docs don't say so.

findings.title: The WS event takes `status` from the bus event and `needs_restart` from the registry, so the two can disagree
findings.why_it_matters: `on_app_state_changed` copies `status` from the event payload and adds `needs_restart` from `resolve_instance_info` at dispatch time (runtime_query_service.py:212-232). D4 says no reader combines entry and record on its own, but the dispatcher does. A payload can say `running` (or `stopping`) plus `needs_restart`, while REST says FAILED. The frontend treats a seen event as authoritative for its index (`instanceLiveNeedsRestart`, app-data.ts:186-193; use-websocket.ts:146), so the store holds a status and a flag from different moments until the next refetch. In a related case, if the FAILED outcome event fails to send, `send_outcome_event` only logs it (app_lifecycle_instances.py:132ff). The store entry then keeps its pre-flag status with `needs_restart: null`, and because the entry shadows the REST row's flag, a refetch doesn't correct the per-instance badge. The wire docstring (ws.py:25-27) doesn't say that `status` may disagree with the flag.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: the WS event's status can briefly disagree with its flag, and a dropped FAILED event leaves a stale per-instance badge until the page reloads.
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation: the WS event's status can briefly disagree with its flag, and a dropped FAILED event leaves a stale per-instance badge until the page reloads.

findings.title: A failed init now holds the app-key lock for up to the full entry deadline, not the old 5 s cleanup bound
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: users with many failing apps or a wedged DB worker; in a typical single-user setup this is a delay, not an outage. The removed `cleanup_failed_instance` capped listener/job removal at a small setting. Now a failed init runs the full coordinated shutdown under `entry_deadline_seconds` (the stop-stage length, config/models.py:339), including Bus/Scheduler DB retirement, all under the app-key lock. If the DB worker wedges, the teardown uses the whole entry deadline and then spends another 5 s walking away. `initialize_instances` runs instances one after another (app_lifecycle_instances.py:84-95), so N failing instances multiply that during bootstrap. This is the shape the ledger ratified: the Summary (design.md:15-16) and the Assumed 134 D19 (design.md:319) put init-failure teardown under the entry deadline, and a runtime stop already holds the lock under the same deadline. D2's 5 s constant covers only the walk-away step.
findings.chosen: Side A: Keep the entry deadline

findings.title: `get_full_snapshot` leaves out apps removed from config that are still flagged, so boot issues miss them
findings.why_it_matters: `get_snapshot` enumerates `[*_instances, *_needs_restart]` (app_registry.py:358), and `overlay_runtime_state` renders orphaned flagged apps through `build_orphaned_flag_info`. `get_full_snapshot` iterates only `self._manifests` (app_registry.py:371-380). Its only caller is `get_boot_issues` (runtime_query_service.py:433), so a flagged app later removed from config never appears as a boot issue. Correcting the critic's scope: `GET /api/apps` builds its own tally from the overlay (routes/apps.py:392-399), so the app list's `status_counts`/`total` and the CLI do include the orphan. Only the boot-issues surface misses it. No test covers the orphan in `get_full_snapshot`.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an app removed from config while flagged is missing from boot issues and appears only in the app list, CLI and badge.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an app removed from config while flagged is missing from boot issues and appears only in the app list, CLI and badge.

findings.title: An exception after `unregister_app` in `shutdown_instance` makes the instance vanish with no failure entry, flag or event
findings.why_it_matters: `shutdown_instance` calls `unregister_app` (app_lifecycle_instances.py:245) outside the `try` that wraps the teardown (lines 230-243). In `settle_failed_stop`, `describe_left_running` and the ERROR log run before `record_failure` and the flag (lines 342-361). If anything there raises, the entry is already gone, nothing is recorded, and the exception escapes. The index then renders as a STOPPED placeholder while work may still run. The ledger accepts Finding 8 ("an exception inside `shutdown_instance` outside the coordinator can ... leave an untorn-down one unflagged", design.md:305-306). This case is the same class with a worse display: the instance shows STOPPED rather than staying FAILED.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a helper that raises after the unregister leaves the index looking STOPPED (an extension of accepted Finding 8).
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a helper that raises after the unregister leaves the index looking STOPPED (an extension of accepted Finding 8).

findings.title: `NeedsRestart.reason`, which doubles as the fallback `error_message`, isn't documented as display-only text
findings.why_it_matters: `resolve_instance_info` fills `error_message` with `record.info.reason` when the entry has none (app_registry.py:181-186), as D4 ratified. A released client can't know to read `needs_restart`, so `error_message` is the only signal it sees, now with synthesized text and no traceback. The `reason` docstring (wire apps.py:19-20) describes the content but doesn't say the wording is unstable, so a client that parses it would break silently when the wording changes.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `reason` has no stability statement, like the other free-text wire fields.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: `reason` has no stability statement, like the other free-text wire fields.

findings.title: `CLEANUP_TIMED_OUT` treated as diagnostic hides work that cleanup left running
`appNeedsRestart`'s max merge can show a count with no reason because the server count covers indices the row doesn't list
A second flag at an index is silently dropped, losing the later instance's pending tasks
A re-create over a flagged index produces FAILED events and rows for a live replacement
